result:
At 4:17 every morning, the city briefly forgot what it was supposed to be.

The buses stopped groaning. The bakeries had not yet begun their warm, yeasty arguments with the dark. Even the traffic lights seemed embarrassed by their own persistence, changing from red to green for nobody at all.

Mara liked that hour because it belonged to no one.

She would carry her mug to the fire escape and sit beneath the rusted satellite dish, listening to the rooftop water tanks creak as they cooled. From there, the buildings looked less like homes than ships: windows glowing in scattered constellations, antennas pointing toward some invisible shore.

One morning, she noticed a light in the apartment across the alley.

It was a small blue light, steady and pale. It appeared in a window that had been dark for as long as she could remember.

Mara watched it for three mornings.

On the fourth, a figure appeared behind the glass. An old man, perhaps, though distance made age difficult. He raised one hand—not waving, exactly, but offering a gesture of recognition.

Mara lifted her mug.

The next morning, there were two blue lights.

The morning after that, three.

Soon, lights began appearing throughout the city: in vacant offices, sealed subway stations, the upper floors of abandoned hotels. They did not flicker or pulse. They simply shone, calm and unwavering, as if someone had opened a door onto the color of deep water.

People invented explanations. A new communications system. A prank. A government experiment. A warning from space. The newspapers printed diagrams, interviews, timelines. Scientists examined the lights and found no heat, no radiation, no source.

But Mara knew what they were.

They were proof that someone, somewhere, was awake.

Years later, when the city had grown taller and the fire escapes had been replaced by elegant balconies, children would ask her if the lights had ever gone away.

“No,” she would tell them. “We just learned how to see them.”

And every morning at 4:17, she would stand by the window with her mug, looking out across the rooftops as the blue lights gathered in the dark—quiet as stars, patient as breath.
